facts.text: There are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.
A spoonful of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tons.
Light from the Andromeda galaxy left home before our species existed.
The cosmic microwave background is a fossil glow from 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
Most of the universe is invisible to us — only 5% is ordinary matter.
Galaxies are not still; they fall through the void in slow, vast currents.
If you could fold space, the nearest star would still be unspeakably far.
The cosmos has no center. Every point believes itself the middle.
Our galaxy is a spiral with arms named Perseus, Sagittarius, and Orion.
At the heart of the Milky Way sleeps a black hole called Sagittarius A*.
It takes the Sun 230 million years to circle the galactic center once.
The dark lanes you see are not empty — they are clouds of cold dust.
Billions of rogue planets drift between the stars, untethered.
Andromeda is rushing toward us at 110 kilometers per second.
The Milky Way will collide with Andromeda in roughly 4.5 billion years.
Most of the galaxy's mass is invisible halo — dark matter we cannot touch.
The Sun contains 99.8% of the mass of the Solar System.
Jupiter shields the inner planets from countless stray comets.
A day on Venus is longer than its year.
Saturn's rings are mostly ice — they would float in a bathtub.
Pluto's heart-shaped plain is named Tombaugh Regio.
Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a frozen archive of the early system.
The Oort Cloud is a sphere of icy bodies a light-year across.
Voyager 1 has left the Sun's bubble and now drifts in interstellar space.
Earth is the only world we know where rain falls and rivers run.
The Moon is slowly drifting away — about 3.8 cm per year.
There is more fresh water in the atmosphere than in all the rivers combined.
Lightning strikes the planet about 8 million times each day.
The deepest part of the ocean would swallow Mount Everest whole.
Earth's magnetic field flips polarity every few hundred thousand years.
Most of the oxygen you breathe comes from ocean plankton.
If Earth were the size of an apple, its atmosphere would be thinner than the skin.
Trees in a forest share sugar and warnings through underground fungal threads.
A single mature oak can host more than 2,000 species in its lifetime.
Forests breathe — global CO2 dips every northern summer.
The smell of rain on dry leaves is called petrichor.
Some aspen groves are a single organism with thousands of trunks.
Owls fly in near-silence thanks to fringed feather edges.
Moss has no roots — it drinks straight from the air.
A teaspoon of forest soil can hold a billion living things.
Inside each leaf, chloroplasts catch photons and weave them into sugar.
Veins in a leaf branch by the same rule as rivers and lightning.
Stomata on the underside of leaves open and close like tiny mouths.
Autumn color is not painted on — it is revealed when green retreats.
A leaf is mostly water, held in place by an architecture of cellulose.
Photosynthesis is the slow theft of light from a star 150 million km away.
Some leaves track the Sun across the sky each day.
Every breath you take has passed through a leaf at least once.
